work-organization.text: Photographic investigation and publicity could expose a disputed workplace scene. Applying age and hour rules required a separate system of reliable records, certificates and inspection. Neither a reform image nor the existence of a statute alone proves workers’ ages or effective protection.

name: A child in a cotton mill: photograph and caption
geographicPrecision: Named mill town from Hine’s caption, not the child’s home address.

interval.label: 3 December 1908

question: What does a photograph show, and what does its caption claim?
summary: A photograph, its caption and an inspection report reveal different kinds of work. Hine’s mill scene became part of a reform campaign; the caption reports an overseer’s denial. Later officials checked age evidence and inspected workplaces to apply particular rules. Neither the child’s age nor effective protection follows from the image alone.

sections.title: Machinery, a person and a chosen view
sections.text: A young figure stands in an aisle between long rows of spinning machinery. The repeated machine parts fill much of the image, while windows light one side of the room. Comparing the person’s height with the equipment makes the setting’s scale visible. Hine chose where to stand and when to expose the photograph. The supplied view documents this arrangement at one moment; it does not let us watch a complete task or reconstruct a working day.

sections.title: Investigation also required circulation
sections.text: The National Child Labor Committee employed Hine for investigative and photographic work from 1908. Photographs travelled through reports, the organization’s publications, newspapers, slide shows and exhibits. Making a case involved recording conditions and arranging evidence for audiences who might never enter the workplace. The Library of Congress describes Hine taking charge of the exhibits department in 1913. Photography belonged to a continuing campaign, alongside writing and display work; one image cannot measure the campaign’s reach or its effects.

citations.locator: Background and Scope: hiring, distribution and exhibits

sections.title: A caption records a contested explanation
sections.text: The selected caption says the child was tending her sides of the machinery, then reports an overseer saying, “She just happened in.” That is a conversation recorded in the campaign’s account, rather than speech audible in the photograph. Another Mollahan caption, dated the same day, identifies a group as spinners and doffers and names Sara R. Hine as witness. Together these records make a small evidence series: they show how work was described, without verifying ages or counting every child employed.

sections.title: A rule needed records and inspectors
sections.text: The 1916 Keating-Owen Act addressed interstate and foreign shipment of specified products made under prohibited age or hour conditions. It authorized workplace inspections and provided for age certificates. The act took effect in September 1917. The Children’s Bureau’s later administration report explains why issuing a certificate was a job of checking evidence: a paper approved on unreliable information could leave inspectors having to establish age again. A statutory limit, a document and a verified fact were different things.

sections.title: Inspection gives a bounded comparison
sections.text: In its spring 1918 South Carolina inspections, the Bureau reported twenty children under fourteen employed in nine of sixty-four establishments visited. It separately recorded missing federal certificates. These are findings from an inspected sample, not a statewide census or identification of this child ten years earlier. The act was declared unconstitutional in June 1918; later visits and state arrangements did not simply disappear. Following changes in working conditions therefore requires dated inspection evidence as well as photographs and the text of a law.

deeperReading.title: The caption is evidence with its own history
deeperReading.text: The Library of Congress transcribed titles, places and dates from caption cards received with the NCLC collection. Its collection account does not establish precisely who compiled every card. Typed strips, handwritten additions and later institutional annotations could share the same surface. Some cards were prepared after the photograph, or described a later revisit. The selected account credits a witness and preserves a reported denial, but neither feature independently checks every statement. The child’s own explanation, a verified age record and a complete employment history remain absent. Reading the caption critically does not require discarding it; it means naming whose account supplies each claim.

deeperReading.title: A series expands questions without becoming a census
deeperReading.text: A second caption can identify another kind of view or another description of work. It cannot turn a deliberately assembled reform collection into a random sample. The Library’s discussion of Hine’s technique also draws attention to choices of framing and focus across other photographs; those examples are not measurements of this image’s camera settings. Finefield’s later account shows students combining photographs with other records to investigate questions. Here, the enforcement report supplies a different source series with stated places, dates and administrative categories. Its authors were describing their own institution’s work, and missing papers were not automatically proof of underage employment. Comparing these sources reveals how claims were made and checked while keeping their populations, purposes and dates distinct.

evidenceReading.title: A scene, related captions and an enforcement record
evidenceReading.introduction: The following are visible observations and editorial paraphrases of identified records. The companion photograph itself is not supplied or newly inspected; its indexed caption title forms the second written record.

items.label: Visible machinery; a reported conversation
items.text: The supplied photograph shows a young figure beside spinning machinery. Its caption reports the overseer saying, “She just happened in,” after the picture was taken.
items.interpretation: The machinery and relative scale can be examined directly. The denial depends on the caption’s account of a conversation. Neither provides a verified birth date, wage, full working day or the child’s own testimony. The caption’s argument should not become an invented biography.

citations.locator: Actual local photograph; indexed caption title, Hine 358

items.label: A second caption gives a group description
items.text: LOC item 2018674903 describes spinners and doffers at Mollahan Mills, dates the caption 3 December 1908 and names Sara R. Hine as witness.
items.interpretation: This supplies a related, separately identified record; it does not establish that the selected child appears in another view. A title naming occupations is evidence of how the group was described. Its assertion about other small workers does not verify their ages or establish a workforce count. Only indexed caption text was accessible in this consultation.

items.label: A legal standard and an observed sample answer different questions
items.text: The 1916 act authorized inspection and age certificates. The Bureau’s 1921 report records underage employment and missing federal certificates as separate findings in its spring 1918 South Carolina inspection sample.
items.interpretation: The law establishes a prescribed rule; the report describes particular administrative findings. Their difference makes enforcement assessable. Neither retrospectively proves the selected child’s age or that one photograph caused legislation. The report was read in HTML transcription; its linked PDF was unavailable.

familyActivity.title: What would you need to check?
steps: Find the person, the aisle and one repeated part of the machinery. Write one observation that another reader can point to in this photograph.
Read the source capsule. Put the overseer’s reported explanation and the known photograph date in a caption column. Leave the child’s exact age unknown.
Compare the caption’s account with the later certificate problem. Explain why having a paper and checking its evidence are different tasks.
Make one supported claim and name one further record you would seek to investigate age or hours. Do not estimate the child’s age from appearance.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: the catalogue dates this photograph to 3 December 1908 at Mollahan Mills, Newberry. Its caption reports that an overseer denied the child was working. A separate caption describes a group at that mill as spinners and doffers. These records do not verify this child’s exact age or hours. A later Children’s Bureau report explains that age certificates based on unreliable evidence could require inspectors to check ages again. A dated birth record could help investigate age; a dated work or inspection record could help investigate hours. None is supplied for this child.

review.scope: The unchanged photograph, a bounded indexed-caption series and selected primary federal administration evidence, with distinct campaign/legal/inspection clocks and a supplied family activity.
limitations: The complete 3 December 1908 case interval, identity, coordinates, older claims/dimensions, object order and original image bytes remain intact. No child name, exact age, hours, pay, biography or image-to-legislation causation recovered.

The 1921 report was read at selected HTML transcription/OCR scope; its linked PDF returned a maintenance page. Its inspection sample and institutional self-account are not a statewide census, independent outcome evaluation or identification of the 1908 child.
